newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - In classical music world, looks count.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - In classical music world, looks count.

text.p: Sara Sant'Ambrogio plucks the base of her cello, taut arms straining as they move rapidly along the instrument, her eyes focused somewhere in the distance and her mind in a zone of intense concentration.

A few feet away violinist Adela Pena opens and closes her eyes and sways with her instrument's sound, free to move in a way a cellist cannot. Set back and between the pair is Erika Nickrenz, wedged in an observation post-like position, stabbing at the keys of a piano that acts as the power source in this modest apartment on Manhattan's Upper West Side.

This is Eroica Trio at work, an all-female, 30-something classical music ensemble capping another five-hour daily rehearsal. Their neighbours would be the first to tell you: This chamber music trio does not play softly, preferring to boom with sound enough to fill a concert hall.
"When people think of chamber music they think of soft and pretty. When we play, it is in your face," Sant'Ambrogio said.

Since 1986, when the trio formed at the Julliard School, the group has climbed steadily in the rarified ranks of classical music and has gained wide attention from something rarely associated with chamber music -- sex appeal.

In 1991, the trio that was named for Beethoven's Third Symphony won the Naumburg Chamber Music Award, an honour not unlike winning an Oscar and which, like filmdom's equivalent, goes by the simple moniker, the Naumburg.

With as much bottled energy as anyone could possess, the women describe their dedication to music and even more to the idea of being the best at their individual crafts, the top pianist, top violinist and top cellist of their time.
AND THEY LOOK GOOD TOO

And, importantly, they are not timid about putting their attractive looks into the marketing mix, a natural move for a group most concerned with enticing new fans to a musical form suffering from terminal stodginess, at least in their eyes.

"We wanted to sell out this hall we were playing in Colorado. So we took our flashiest picture and advertised it as a night of romance, Dvorak, Mahler. ... In the picture we wore our short black dresses and put the signs up in places you usually don't see them like supermarkets, the rodeo, old time saloons," Nickrenz said.

Sure enough, many in the crowd were not typical chamber music-goers. The audience included "real cowboys," Nickrenz said, who stomped their spurs in time with the tunes. The lesson the threesome learned was not that sex appeal was more important than music but that, as Sant'Ambrogio said, "They were there for the babes but they loved the music and asked where they could go to hear more."

She said the trio wanted to be the conduit for igniting interest in classical music, to sell records, cross over into the mainstream by appearing in videos, setting up a web site, performing in non-traditional venues and appearing in movies, not to mention attracting new chamber trio compositions.
CLASSICAL MUSIC'S MICHAEL JORDAN

As they see it, they can be a classical music version of basketball star Michael Jordan, transcending their field and tearing down what they call "artifical barriers" that keep young people away from the art form.
"We'd like to do that for classical music, bring it back into the vernacular, as part of our lives and our culture, we think we can do it," Sant'Ambrogio said.
By being the oddball -- in this case an all-female chamber music trio in a historically male domain -- the opportunities available to the trio may indeed go beyond the norm.
"We want our audiences to go home and feel that every part of their soul has been touched. That you are completely satisfied and satiated. We feel that way every time," Sant'Ambrogio said.

"You can be attractive and you can enjoy being sexy and liking how you feel. We feel pretty good about how we look, but we also worked our butts off. We're very disciplined and we've now climbed up a ladder in a very difficult, male-dominated field," she added.
Recent appearances in Europe for the Distinctive Debuts' international series and a well-received recital at Carnegie Hall's prestigious Weill Recital Hall continued the ascent.
"We have proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that we are the top players of our generation," Sant'Ambrogio said.
Just ask the cowboys.
